title: Load balancers deep
scopeHtml: Scope: L4 vs L7, balancing algorithms, sticky sessions, health checks, connection draining, LB high availability, global LB and anycast, with a sizing example.

notes.title: Why a load balancer and what it does
notes.html:
A load balancer (LB) is the single front door that spreads traffic over many servers, hides failures, and lets you change servers without clients noticing. It gives you: capacity (add servers), availability (skip dead ones), and flexibility (deploy gradually, route by path).

Worked example. Peak traffic 12,000 requests/s, one app server handles 1,500/s at 60% target CPU. You need 12,000 / 1,500 = 8 servers, plus one spare per AZ for failure: with 3 AZs run 12 servers (4 per AZ), so losing a whole AZ leaves 8, enough. The LB hides which of 12 answered.

Industry examples. AWS ALB/NLB, GCP Cloud Load Balancing, Azure Front Door, NGINX, HAProxy, Envoy; hardware F5. Google's Maglev and Meta's Katran are software L4 LBs on commodity servers.

Everyday analogy. The head waiter at a restaurant who seats guests at open tables, stops using a table with a broken chair, and lets you add new tables without telling the guests.

Common interview traps.

  • Drawing a single LB box with no mention of its own redundancy.
  • No capacity maths for the pool or for N+1 / AZ loss.
  • Treating the LB as free: it has throughput, connection and TLS limits.

notes.title: L4 vs L7 load balancing
notes.html:
An L4 balancer works on TCP/UDP connections; an L7 balancer understands HTTP.

  • L4: sees IP, port. Picks a backend at connection start and forwards packets (NAT or direct server return). Very fast (millions of packets/s per box), low latency (microseconds), protocol-agnostic (databases, MQTT, gRPC as raw TCP). Cannot look at URLs, cookies, or retry on 5xx.
  • L7: terminates the client connection, parses requests, can route by host/path/header/cookie, do TLS termination, rewrite, rate-limit, retry, canary by weight, add auth, and balance each request (not each connection). Costs more CPU (maybe 10x fewer requests/s per box) and adds about 0.1 to 1 ms.
L4 (NLB, Maglev, LVS) L7 (ALB, Nginx, Envoy)
Unit balanced connection request
Sees IP/port URL, headers, cookies
TLS passthrough or terminate terminate usually
Speed very high lower
Extras static IP, preserves source IP routing, retries, WAF, gRPC-aware

Decision gravity. Most apps want L7 (routing, observability). L4 in front of an L7 fleet is the large-scale pattern: L4 gives stable IPs and absorbs floods, L7 does the smart work. Switching later is mostly a DNS/endpoint change, so it is reversible, but clients with hard-coded IPs or allow-lists make the L4 static IP a sticky commitment.

Industry examples. Google's front end: Maglev (L4) then GFE (L7). Facebook: Katran (L4, XDP/eBPF) then Proxygen/Envoy-style L7. Cloudflare and AWS use the same layered idea. gRPC needs L7 (or client-side balancing) because one long HTTP/2 connection otherwise pins to one backend.

Everyday analogy. L4 is a postal sorting machine reading only the postcode; L7 is a clerk who opens the letter and routes by what it says.

Common interview traps.

  • Using L4 with gRPC/HTTP2 and getting one hot backend.
  • Forgetting the client's real IP is hidden behind L7 (use X-Forwarded-For or Proxy Protocol).
  • Saying L7 is always better; L4 is simpler and faster for non-HTTP.

notes.title: Load balancing algorithms
notes.html:
The algorithm decides which backend gets the next request. Pick based on request cost variation, connection length and whether you need affinity.

  • Round robin / weighted round robin: rotate; weights for unequal machines. Good when requests are similar and short.
  • Least connections / least outstanding requests: send to the backend with the fewest active ones. Better when request time varies a lot or connections are long (WebSockets, uploads).
  • Power of two choices (P2C): pick 2 random backends, send to the less loaded. Almost as good as full least-loaded with no global state; used by Envoy, NGINX (random two), Twitter Finagle. Avoids the herd problem where everyone picks the same "least loaded" server between load updates.
  • IP hash / consistent hashing: same key (client IP, user ID, URL) to the same backend; adding/removing a backend moves only about 1/N of keys. Good for caches (CDN, memcached proxies), sharded services. Bounded-load consistent hashing (Google paper, used in HAProxy, Vimeo) caps hotspots.
  • Random: simple, surprisingly good at scale.
  • Latency-aware / peak EWMA: weight by recent response time; slow nodes get less.

Worked example. 2 servers, 1,000 requests; 10% of requests take 2 s and others 20 ms. Round robin can by chance stack slow requests on one server (queue grows, p99 explodes) while the other idles. Least outstanding requests keeps both queues near equal. With 100 LB nodes each tracking only local counts, P2C still keeps the max queue length near log log N instead of log N.

Config example (nginx).

# upstream pool: least_conn with weights and failure handling
# upstream api {
#   least_conn;
#   server 10.0.1.10:8080 weight=3 max_fails=3 fail_timeout=10s;
#   server 10.0.1.11:8080 weight=1 max_fails=3 fail_timeout=10s;
#   keepalive 64;
# }

Industry examples. Envoy defaults to round robin and offers least request (P2C), ring hash, Maglev hash. AWS ALB offers round robin and least outstanding requests. Memcached/Redis clients and CDNs use consistent hashing.

Decision gravity. Algorithm is a reversible config. Consistent hashing becomes semi-sticky: data placement may depend on it (local caches warm), so changing it causes a cold cache stampede.

Everyday analogy. Supermarket checkouts: round robin is "next in line goes to lane 1, 2, 3..." even if lane 2 has a full trolley; least connections is "join the shortest queue".

Common interview traps.

  • Recommending round robin for long-lived connections.
  • Hashing on IP behind a NAT: thousands of users share one IP and hit one backend.
  • Not knowing consistent hashing's remapping property.

notes.title: Sticky sessions and session affinity
notes.html:
Stickiness sends the same client to the same backend. Methods: cookie set by the LB (AWSALB), source-IP hash, or a header/user-ID hash.

Why people use it: legacy apps with in-memory sessions, local caches that warm per user, WebSocket reconnect to the same node. Why to avoid it: it breaks even load (a heavy user pins a node), the session dies with the server, and rolling deploys lose sessions. Better: stateless servers with a shared store (Redis) or signed tokens. Use stickiness only as an optimisation where state is rebuildable.

Worked example. 10,000 users, 10 servers. Without stickiness each server has about 1,000 users. A power user group (a corporate NAT of 2,000 users) with IP-hash lands entirely on one server: 3,000 users there versus 800 elsewhere, 3.75x the load.

Industry examples. Early shopping carts in Java servlet containers used sticky sessions with Tomcat replication; modern shops use Redis or JWT. Gaming and chat edge servers use sticky routing by room or user ID (consistent hashing) deliberately.

Decision gravity. Starting sticky is easy; removing it later needs a state-externalisation project. If you must be sticky, design it as a hint, not as a requirement for correctness.

Everyday analogy. Always seeing the same doctor: nice continuity, but if she is on leave or overbooked, you wait or lose your notes unless they are in the shared file.

Common interview traps.

  • Using IP hash behind a corporate NAT or mobile carrier NAT.
  • Forgetting that a sticky node failure loses in-memory state.
  • Combining stickiness with autoscaling scale-in that kills the pinned node.

notes.title: Health checks
notes.html:
Health checks let the LB find dead or sick backends and stop sending them traffic. Two kinds:

  • Active: LB probes GET /health every N seconds. Parameters: interval, timeout, unhealthy threshold, healthy threshold.
  • Passive (outlier detection): LB watches real traffic; after e.g. 5 consecutive 5xx or connection resets, eject the node for 30 s (Envoy outlier detection, nginx max_fails).

Typical values: interval 10 s, timeout 3 s, unhealthy after 3 failures (30 s to detect), healthy after 2 successes. Faster interval means faster detection but more probe load and more flapping.

What should /health check? Shallow (process is up, returns 200) vs deep (checks DB, cache). Danger of deep checks: if the shared database hiccups, every server fails its check, the LB removes all of them, and a minor blip becomes a total outage. Common compromise: liveness (is the process alive) and readiness (can it serve now) kept separate, deep dependency checks only affect readiness of that instance for its own local problems, with the LB configured with fail-open / panic mode (Envoy: if more than 50% hosts are unhealthy, ignore health status and send to all).

# Kubernetes probes, typical values
readinessProbe:
  httpGet: { path: /ready, port: 8080 }
  periodSeconds: 5
  failureThreshold: 3
livenessProbe:
  httpGet: { path: /live, port: 8080 }
  periodSeconds: 10
  failureThreshold: 6
startupProbe:
  httpGet: { path: /live, port: 8080 }
  failureThreshold: 30
  periodSeconds: 2

Production incident pattern. A slow dependency makes the health endpoint time out; all nodes marked unhealthy together; 503s everywhere although nodes could serve cached data. Metric: healthy host count dropping to 0 while CPU is low. Another: restart loop from an overly strict liveness probe on a slow-starting JVM (needs a startup probe).

Industry examples. AWS ALB target group health checks, GCP, Envoy outlier detection and panic threshold, Kubernetes readiness gating of Service endpoints.

Everyday analogy. A shop manager who checks every few minutes that each till works, but does not close the whole shop because the card network is briefly slow.

Common interview traps.

  • Deep health checks that cascade a dependency failure to all nodes.
  • Using liveness probes that kill pods under load, making overload worse.
  • Forgetting warm-up: sending full traffic to a freshly started cold JVM (use slow start, slow_start / ALB slow start mode).

notes.title: Connection draining and graceful deploys
notes.html:
Draining (deregistration delay) means a backend that is leaving stops getting new requests but is allowed to finish the ones in flight. Without it, a deploy or scale-in cuts requests in half: clients see 502/connection reset.

Correct shutdown sequence:

  1. Mark the instance as draining (LB stops new requests). In Kubernetes: pod removed from endpoints.
  2. Wait for in-flight requests to finish, up to a timeout (ALB deregistration delay default 300 s; set to the max request time plus margin, e.g. 30 s for APIs).
  3. App receives SIGTERM, stops accepting, finishes work, closes idle connections, exits.
  4. If still running after the grace period, SIGKILL.

A classic gotcha in Kubernetes: the endpoint removal and SIGTERM race. Some LBs and kube-proxy keep sending traffic for a few seconds after SIGTERM, so add a preStop sleep of 5 to 15 s before shutting down.

# Kubernetes graceful shutdown
spec:
  terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 45
  containers:
  - name: api
    lifecycle:
      preStop:
        exec: { command: ["sleep", "10"] }   # let LB/endpoints catch up

Worked example. Rolling deploy of 20 pods, each handles 200 requests/s with a p99 of 400 ms and 2% of requests being 20 s uploads. A drain of 30 s completes nearly everything; a drain of 0 s drops about 80 requests per pod instantly (in flight) = 1,600 errors across the deploy, visible as a spike in 5xx every release.

Industry examples. AWS ELB connection draining, Envoy drain_time, NGINX graceful reload (nginx -s reload keeps old workers until they finish), Kubernetes terminationGracePeriodSeconds, GKE and Argo Rollouts for progressive delivery. Long-lived connections (WebSocket) need a "go away" message (HTTP/2 GOAWAY) so clients reconnect elsewhere gradually.

Decision gravity. Setting this up is cheap and reversible; skipping it silently costs reliability on every deploy.

Everyday analogy. A restaurant announcing "last orders": no new guests, but those already seated finish their meal before the lights go off.

Common interview traps.

  • Deploys that cause a burst of 502s because of no drain or no preStop delay.
  • Drain timeout shorter than the longest request.
  • Reconnect storms when a draining server drops all WebSockets at once (spread with jitter).

notes.title: Making the load balancer itself highly available
notes.html:
The LB is a single point of failure unless you design it not to be. Patterns:

  1. Active-passive pair with a floating (virtual) IP: keepalived/VRRP; standby takes the IP in about 1 to 3 s on failure. Wastes half the capacity.
  2. Active-active behind DNS: several LB IPs in one DNS name (cloud LBs do this per AZ). Failover bounded by DNS TTL and client behaviour.
  3. Active-active with ECMP: the network router spreads flows over many L4 LB machines using equal-cost multi-path routing; LBs announce the VIP via BGP. Maglev and Katran use consistent hashing so that when an LB node fails, existing connections mostly keep the same backend.
  4. Managed cloud LB: AWS ALB/NLB scale automatically across AZs; you pay per LCU/GB.

Capacity notes: an L7 LB needs warm-up, and sudden 10x traffic can exceed what it has scaled to (AWS suggests pre-warming for planned spikes; ALB scales roughly with load over minutes). Limits to know: connections per node, TLS handshakes/s, bandwidth, ephemeral ports to backends (about 64k per backend IP:port, a cause of 502/connect failures at high rates without keepalive to backends).

Industry examples. Google Maglev (ECMP + consistent hashing, 10 Gbps+ per machine class), Meta Katran (XDP), GitHub's GLB director (consistent hash with a two-tier design), AWS NLB (static IPs per AZ).

Decision gravity. Self-managing LBs is an operations commitment; managed LBs are the default. Moving between them is a DNS cutover: reversible but needs care with TTL and allow-lists of IPs.

Everyday analogy. Instead of one receptionist at the door, have several at several doors, with a sign saying which doors are open.

Common interview traps.

  • Active-passive without testing failover.
  • Forgetting the LB's own connection/port limits.
  • Ignoring that DNS-based failover is slow.

notes.title: Global load balancing and anycast
notes.html:
Global load balancing sends users to the best region or data centre, not just the best server. Mechanisms:

  • DNS-based GSLB: return the IP of the nearest/healthy region (latency, geo, weighted, failover). Simple; limited by DNS TTL and resolver location.
  • Anycast: every region announces the same IP; BGP delivers users to the nearest. Quick failover when a site withdraws its route (seconds); used by CDNs and AWS Global Accelerator (2 static anycast IPs, traffic enters AWS network at the nearest edge and rides the private backbone to the region).
  • Global L7 front door: Google Cloud's single anycast VIP for all regions, Azure Front Door, Cloudflare. Terminates TLS at the edge close to the user (short handshake), then routes over a warm connection to the best healthy region.

What a global design must also solve: data locality (user data in region, replicate or route writes to a home region), failover capacity (if Region A dies, B must have headroom, typically run each region at 50 to 60% so the remaining can absorb), health at region level, and traffic shifting (drain a region gradually, 10% steps).

Worked example. Two regions, each 100k requests/s peak and 50k capacity headroom needed for failover: if each region runs at 50% of its max capacity (200k max), then on a regional failure the survivor must absorb 200k, exactly its limit. Active-active with N regions needs only 1/(N-1) extra headroom: with 3 regions you need each at 66% maximum utilisation to survive one loss.

Industry examples. Netflix evacuates a region by shifting traffic via DNS/Zuul ("regional evacuation" drills with Chaos Kong). Google uses one global VIP with Maglev + GFE. Cloudflare anycast across 300+ cities. AWS Route 53 latency + health checks and Global Accelerator.

Decision gravity. Going multi-region is a large one-way door for data: write routing, conflict resolution and cost double. Start with CDN + single region + a warm standby; add active-active only when SLA or latency demands.

Everyday analogy. A national airline's call centre: one number everywhere, routed to the nearest open office, with the other offices ready to take over if one closes.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying "multi-region" without addressing data and write conflicts.
  • No spare capacity in the surviving region.
  • Relying only on DNS TTL for failover.

notes.title: Choosing and sizing: a worked design
notes.html:
Scenario. A food-ordering API: 20k requests/s peak, mix of REST (short) and a tracking WebSocket (long), users across India, mobile clients.

Decisions:

  1. Edge: CDN/anycast edge terminates TLS and speaks h2/h3 to phones (short handshakes), static content cached.
  2. Regional L7 LB (ALB/Envoy): path routing /api/*, /track/ws; least outstanding requests for API, least connections for WebSocket target group; 3 AZs; health check /ready interval 10 s, unhealthy 3, healthy 2; deregistration delay 30 s; slow start 30 s.
  3. Pool size: 20k / 1,500 per server = 14 at 100%; at 60% target CPU run 23, rounded to 24 (8 per AZ) so losing one AZ leaves 16 which handles 24k at 100% (acceptable for short failover with autoscaling).
  4. WebSockets: 500k concurrent connections at about 20 KB each = 10 GB of memory; spread over 12 tracking nodes; use "go away + jitter" on deploys.
  5. Observability: alert on target 5xx rate, healthy host count, p99 latency, LB 5xx versus target 5xx (distinguishes LB-generated 502/503/504 from app errors), active connections, rejected connections, surge queue length.

Production incident patterns.

  • LB 502 vs 504: 502 = bad response/connection reset by backend (often idle-timeout mismatch: LB idle 60 s, backend keep-alive 5 s closes first, so set backend keep-alive higher than LB idle timeout), 504 = backend too slow.
  • Retry storms: the LB or client retries a failing backend and doubles load; use retry budgets (Envoy: at most 20% extra) and jittered backoff.
  • Thundering herd after a restart: all caches cold, everything hits the DB. Use slow start and gradual ramp.

Everyday analogy. Planning a stadium: gates, queues, emergency exits and enough staff so that one closed gate doesn't stop the match.

Common interview traps.

  • No capacity maths or AZ-loss headroom.
  • Not distinguishing LB-generated errors from app errors in monitoring.
  • Idle timeout mismatches giving rare, hard-to-reproduce 502s.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• An LB gives capacity, availability and flexibility; size the pool with maths (peak / per-server rate, target utilisation, N+1 per AZ).
  • L4 balances connections fast; L7 balances requests with routing and TLS. Large systems layer L4 in front of L7; gRPC needs L7 or client-side balancing.
  • Algorithms: round robin for uniform short requests, least outstanding requests for variable ones, P2C for distributed LBs, consistent hashing for caches and affinity.
  • Prefer stateless servers; sticky sessions are a fragile optimisation and break with NAT, deploys and failures.
  • Health checks: active and passive, tune interval/threshold, keep checks shallow to avoid cascading, separate liveness from readiness, use panic/fail-open mode, slow start for warm-up.
  • Draining plus preStop delay plus SIGTERM handling makes deploys error-free; match idle timeouts (backend > LB).
  • Make the LB itself redundant (VRRP, ECMP with consistent hashing, managed multi-AZ); global LB uses DNS GSLB or anycast with spare regional capacity and a plan for data locality.

questions.promptHtml: What is the difference between an L4 and an L7 load balancer, and when would you pick each?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It is the most common LB opener; the signal is whether you tie the layer to what the balancer can see and do.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: An L4 balancer works on TCP/UDP connections: it sees IP and port, picks a backend when the connection starts and forwards packets. It is very fast and protocol-agnostic. An L7 balancer terminates the connection, parses HTTP, and balances each request, so it can route by path or header, terminate TLS, retry and canary. I use L7 for web and API traffic, L4 for non-HTTP protocols or as a fast front layer that gives stable IPs and absorbs floods.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
L4 (NLB, Maglev, LVS) L7 (ALB, NGINX, Envoy)
Unit balanced connection request
Sees IP, port URL, headers, cookies
Cost microseconds, millions of packets/s about 0.1 to 1 ms, roughly 10x fewer req/s per box
Extras static IP, source IP kept routing, WAF, retries, rate limit 
Internet -> L4 LB (stable IPs, floods) -> L7 proxy fleet -> Services

A key consequence: with L4, one long HTTP/2 connection pins to one backend, so a gRPC client sees no balancing. L7 balances each request on the connection.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• L4 in front of gRPC and getting a hot backend.
  • Forgetting the client IP is lost behind L7 (use X-Forwarded-For or PROXY protocol).
  • Saying L7 is always better.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How does the backend learn the client IP? -> X-Forwarded-For from L7, PROXY protocol or preserved source IP at L4.
  2. Why layer L4 in front of L7? -> Stable anycast or static IPs, cheap flood absorption, and the L7 fleet can scale behind it.
  3. Can L7 balance a database? -> Not unless it speaks the protocol; Postgres and MQTT are typically L4.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer lists "L4 is faster". The senior links layer to what is visible, names the HTTP/2 pinning problem, and describes the layered production stack.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team put gRPC behind an L4 balancer; one pod took 80 percent of calls until they moved to L7 balancing.

questions.promptHtml: Compare round robin, least connections, power of two choices and consistent hashing. When does each fit?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Algorithm choice shows if you reason from request cost distribution and state needs.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Round robin is simple and fine when requests are similar and short. Least connections or least outstanding requests is better when request time varies or connections are long. Power of two choices picks two random backends and takes the less loaded: nearly as good as global least-loaded without shared state, and it avoids herding. Consistent hashing sends the same key to the same backend, great for caches and sharded services, and moves only about 1/N of keys when backends change.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Round robin ignores load: if 10% of requests take 2 s and the rest 20 ms, by chance slow ones stack on one server and p99 explodes. Least outstanding requests equalises queues. With many LB nodes, each only knows its own counts; if all pick the global minimum from stale data, they herd onto one backend. P2C avoids that: it keeps the maximum queue near log log N rather than log N.

Algorithm     State needed      Good for                        Risk
round robin   none              uniform short requests          slow requests pile up
least conn    per-backend count variable/long requests          herd on new node
P2C           per-backend count distributed LBs (Envoy)         little
hash/ring     none              caches, sharding, affinity      hotspots, cold cache on change

Bounded-load consistent hashing caps the load per node to avoid hotspots.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Round robin for long-lived connections (WebSocket).
  • IP hash behind NAT: thousands of users on one backend.
  • Changing the hashing algorithm without planning for a cold cache.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What happens to keys when a node is added with modulo hashing? -> Almost all keys move; consistent hashing moves about 1/N.
  2. Why is P2C used by Envoy? -> No global state, avoids herd, good tail latency.
  3. How do you handle a heterogeneous fleet? -> Weighted algorithms or latency-aware (peak EWMA).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer defines each. The senior picks by request-time variance and statefulness, and mentions herding and cold-cache effects.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A cache tier moved from modulo to consistent hashing after a node loss emptied the cache and sent 100 percent of reads to the database.

questions.contextHtml:
A B2B web app has 10 backend servers, sticky sessions by source-IP hash. Each normally serves about 1,000 users at 35% CPU. After onboarding a large enterprise customer whose 2,000 employees all egress through one corporate NAT IP, one server (web-7) runs at 95% CPU with p99 of 6 s; the others sit at 30%. Dashboards:

server   active_users   cpu    p99
web-1        ~800       30%   120ms
...
web-7       ~3,000      95%    6.1s

A teammate wants to add 5 more servers.
questions.promptHtml: What is going on and what do you do?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Adds servers (the hash still pins 3,000 users to web-7). Or removes stickiness with no thought about what state lives in memory.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Why are we sticky: in-memory sessions or a warm cache? What breaks if a user lands on another node? Do other large NAT customers exist? Can we put session state in Redis?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Move to cookie-based stickiness (per user, not per IP) or temporarily disable stickiness for this customer's range if state allows; at minimum, spread by cookie.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) IP hash collapses a NAT population onto one backend, (b) one user is abusing, (c) GC or noisy neighbour on web-7, (d) bad health check.
  4. How I'd verify each: log source IP per request, count distinct users per IP, compare with web-7 request rate; check GC logs and CPU steal on web-7; look at LB hash config.
  5. Root cause: 3,000 versus 800 users, a 3.75x load difference, because hashing by IP treats 2,000 people as one client.
  6. Fix: Short term: cookie affinity. Long term: stateless servers with sessions in Redis or signed tokens; stickiness only as a hint (warm cache) where state is rebuildable.
  7. Prevention: Alert on per-backend load skew (max / mean over 1.5); load-test with NAT-shaped traffic.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not more servers; it does not move the hot set. Externalising sessions costs a Redis hop and a project, but removes the failure class including deploy session loss.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Cookie affinity but web-7 dies? -> Users lose in-memory sessions; another reason to externalise.
  • Autoscaling scale-in kills pinned nodes? -> Yes; stickiness plus scale-in logs people out.
  • WebSockets need stickiness? -> Use user or room consistent hashing deliberately, with reconnect logic.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A hospital group on a single NAT address got every user pinned to one node for months before anyone noticed, because average CPU looked fine.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: adds servers.
  • Hire: identifies NAT and IP hash skew, moves to cookie or stateless.
  • Strong hire: quantifies the skew, externalises state, alerts on load imbalance.

questions.contextHtml: 12:04: the primary Postgres failed over (took 35 s). The API cluster of 30 instances sits behind an ALB; the /health endpoint runs SELECT 1 and returns 500 if it fails (timeout 3 s, unhealthy threshold 3, interval 10 s). At 12:05 the ALB shows 0 healthy hosts, all requests get 503. The DB recovered at 12:05 but the service did not recover until 12:09. CPU on the API was 5% the whole time. Endpoints serving cached catalogue data could have worked during the failover.
questions.promptHtml: What happened and how would you redesign health checks?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "The DB was down, so 503s were correct." Misses that the DB blip became a total outage amplified by the health check design, and that recovery was slow.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What does health check verify (deep vs shallow)? What are the thresholds? Does the LB have fail-open behaviour? Which endpoints depend on the DB?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Make the health check return 200 or point the target group to a shallow endpoint; if the LB supports fail-open (panic mode), enable it so traffic goes to all hosts.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) deep check makes all instances unhealthy together, (b) healthy threshold of 2 successes at 10 s keeps them out for another 20 s plus propagation, (c) connection pool needed time to recover, (d) LB bug.
  4. How I'd verify: ALB health check logs and HealthyHostCount going to 0 while CPU low; app logs of /health latency; connection pool metrics after failover.
  5. Root cause: A shared dependency in the health check makes the failure correlated, so the LB removed every host. Outage lasted longer than the DB failure because of the unhealthy and healthy threshold timers plus pool recovery.
  6. Fix: Short term: shallow /health. Long term: separate liveness (process alive) and readiness (can serve, local problems only); DB issues degrade features (cached reads, error on writes) instead of removing nodes; configure panic mode when over 50% unhealthy; tune thresholds.
  7. Prevention: Failure injection of the DB in staging; alert on healthy host count; a rule that health checks never test shared dependencies of all instances.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: A shallow check can send traffic to an instance with a broken local dependency (stale cache, full disk): cover with passive outlier detection. I would not make checks so aggressive that they flap.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• A single instance has a bad DB connection pool. -> Make its readiness local (pool state) so only that instance is ejected.
  • Fail-open sends traffic to truly dead nodes? -> Yes, that is the trade; combined with passive ejection and retries.
  • Liveness probe times out under load? -> It can kill pods and worsen load; keep liveness cheap and use startup probes for slow starts.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A 40-second DB failover became a 6-minute full outage. The fix was removing one line from the health endpoint.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: blames the database.
  • Hire: explains correlated deep checks and proposes shallow plus readiness.
  • Strong hire: threshold math for recovery, panic mode, outlier detection and failure injection.

questions.contextHtml:
Every rolling deploy of a 12-pod API (about 250 requests/s per pod, p99 400 ms, 2% of requests are 20 s uploads) produces a spike of 502s and connection resets, roughly 1,500 failed requests each time. Manifest and behaviour:

spec:
  terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 30
  containers:
  - name: api
    image: api:2.14
    # no lifecycle.preStop
    readinessProbe:
      httpGet: { path: /ready, port: 8080 }
      periodSeconds: 10
      failureThreshold: 3

The app exits immediately on SIGTERM. ALB deregistration delay is 300 s. The dev says "Kubernetes handles it".
questions.promptHtml: Find what is wrong and fix the deploy.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add retries on the client" (hides it), or "increase replicas". Misses the SIGTERM versus endpoint-removal race and in-flight requests.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Does the app handle SIGTERM gracefully? Which LB sits in front (target IP mode vs instance mode)? What is the longest request? Are errors 502 or 504?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Add a preStop sleep of 10 s now; this is a safe manifest change.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) pod gets SIGTERM before the LB stops sending (endpoint propagation lag of seconds), (b) app closes the listener instantly and drops in-flight requests, (c) grace period shorter than the 20 s uploads, (d) probe period too slow to matter.
  4. How I'd verify: correlate 502 timestamps with pod termination; watch LB target deregistration timeline; add a log line at SIGTERM and at last request.
  5. Root cause: The sequence is not "drain, then stop". Traffic still arrives for several seconds after SIGTERM and in-flight requests are killed. 12 pods x about 125 in-flight requests dropped fits the roughly 1,500 failures.
  6. Fix: Add preStop sleep, handle SIGTERM by stopping accept and finishing work, and set terminationGracePeriodSeconds above preStop plus the longest request.
spec:
  terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 60   # preStop 10 + longest request 30 + margin
  containers:
  - name: api
    lifecycle:
      preStop:
        exec: { command: ["sleep", "10"] }

Set the ALB deregistration delay to about 30 s for an API (default 300 s only delays scale-in). 7. Prevention: Deploy test under load with an error budget alert; track 5xx during releases; readiness fails first on shutdown. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: A longer grace period slows deploys. I would not rely on client retries for non-idempotent calls. Long uploads may need presigned direct upload instead of through the API.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• WebSocket connections? -> Send a go-away message and spread reconnects with jitter.
  • Why not maxUnavailable: 0? -> Helps capacity but does not remove the race.
  • Does NGINX reload have the same issue? -> No; old workers finish in-flight requests.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team accepted a 0.3% error blip on every release for a year. A 10-second preStop made releases invisible and the on-call stopped watching deploys.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: adds client retries.
  • Hire: preStop plus SIGTERM handling plus grace period larger than longest request.
  • Strong hire: explains the endpoint propagation race, quantifies dropped in-flight work, tunes deregistration delay and handles WebSockets.

questions.contextHtml: You are asked to size a pool for a ticketing API: peak 18,000 requests/s (flash sales), one server handles 1,500 requests/s at 100% CPU, you want 60% target CPU, 3 AZs. The business states "we must survive losing an AZ during a sale". It also says "the budget is tight". Autoscaling takes about 4 minutes to add capacity.
questions.promptHtml: How many servers do you run and how do you justify it?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: 18,000 / 1,500 = 12 servers. Ignores headroom, AZ loss and slow autoscaling.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Does the SLO need full performance during an AZ loss or degraded? Is 18k a measured peak or a guess? How spiky is the ramp? Can we queue or shed non-critical traffic?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Not an incident; I compute the baseline first.
  3. Hypotheses (options) ranked:
    • Baseline at 100%: 18,000 / 1,500 = 12.
    • At 60% target: 18,000 / (1,500 x 0.6) = 20.
    • AZ loss: with 3 AZs, losing one leaves 2/3 of capacity, so I need N x 2/3 x 900 >= 18,000, N = 30 (10 per AZ).
    • Relax: survivors can run at 100% briefly: 20 servers x 2/3 = 13.3 x 1,500 = 20,000, which handles 18,000 at 90% CPU (acceptable for minutes if the SLO allows).
  4. How I'd verify: load test to find the real per-server rate at p99 target; test AZ failure with a game day.
  5. Root cause (why the simple answer is wrong): capacity must cover utilisation target and failure domain.
  6. Fix (the recommendation): 21 to 24 servers (7 to 8 per AZ) for flash sales: with 24, losing an AZ leaves 16 x 1,500 = 24,000 at 100% for 18,000 load, which is 75% CPU. Pre-scale before the sale because autoscaling takes 4 minutes; scale in after.
  7. Prevention: Scheduled scaling for known events; alerts on healthy hosts per AZ; periodic AZ-failure test.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: 30 servers is safest but 25% more cost; 24 trades a bit of CPU headroom during AZ loss for cost. I would not rely on reactive autoscaling for a spike that arrives in seconds. I'd also rate-limit or queue to protect the pool.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• The LB itself? -> ALB scales over minutes; ask for pre-warming for planned spikes.
  • Two AZs only? -> Losing one leaves 50%, so each AZ must hold the full load: 100% overprovision.
  • Servers per AZ not equal? -> Cross-zone load balancing evens requests but not cost; check data transfer charges.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A flash sale sized as 12 servers at 100% passed testing and died when one AZ degraded mid-sale. Re-sizing with the failure domain cost 80% more but saved the event.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: 12 servers.
  • Hire: includes utilisation target and AZ loss.
  • Strong hire: shows numbers for options, pre-scales for the ramp, and states cost versus risk trade-off.

questions.promptHtml: Explain active and passive health checks, and the difference between liveness, readiness and startup probes. What should /health check?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Bad health checks cause self-inflicted outages. They want a reasoned design, not a copy of defaults.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Active checks are probes the LB sends every few seconds; passive checks watch real traffic and eject a backend after consecutive failures. Liveness asks "should this process be restarted", readiness asks "can it take traffic now", startup protects slow-starting apps from being killed. A health endpoint should be shallow: it must not check a dependency shared by all instances, because then one blip removes every node at once.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Typical timing: interval 10 s, timeout 3 s, unhealthy after 3 failures (30 s to detect), healthy after 2 successes. Faster detection costs more probes and more flapping.

readinessProbe: { httpGet: { path: /ready, port: 8080 }, periodSeconds: 5, failureThreshold: 3 }
livenessProbe:  { httpGet: { path: /live,  port: 8080 }, periodSeconds: 10, failureThreshold: 6 }
startupProbe:   { httpGet: { path: /live,  port: 8080 }, periodSeconds: 2,  failureThreshold: 30 }
  • Liveness should be cheap and about the process only. A liveness probe that fails under load kills pods and makes overload worse.
  • Readiness may include local conditions (warmed cache, pool initialised), and gates the Service endpoint.
  • Panic or fail-open mode (Envoy: ignore health when more than 50% hosts unhealthy) avoids total outage from a correlated false signal.
  • Slow start ramps traffic to a new instance so a cold JVM is not hit with full load.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Deep checks that call the database.
  • Liveness equal to readiness.
  • No slow start; new node gets a full share immediately.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why use passive checks too? -> They react to real failures within one or two requests, not after a 30 s probe window.
  2. A JVM takes 90 s to start; the liveness probe restarts it forever. -> Add a startup probe (30 x 2 s = 60 s, raise it).
  3. When is a deep check okay? -> For a dependency private to one instance, in readiness only, with fail-open protection.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer says "/health returns 200". The senior separates probe types, picks thresholds with detection time math and designs for correlated failure.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A one-line SELECT 1 in the health endpoint turned a 35 s DB failover into a multi-minute total outage.

questions.promptHtml: The load balancer is a single point of failure. How do you make it highly available, and what limits its capacity?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Candidates draw "LB" as a box. Seniors know the LB has failover mechanics, connection limits and warm-up behaviour.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: In cloud I use a managed multi-AZ LB. When self-managing, I run active-passive with VRRP and a floating IP (failover in 1 to 3 s, half the capacity idle), or active-active: several LB IPs in DNS, or ECMP routing where the router spreads flows over many L4 nodes announcing a VIP via BGP. Large L4 systems like Maglev and Katran use consistent hashing so existing connections keep their backend when an LB node dies. I also watch limits: connections, TLS handshakes per second, bandwidth and ephemeral ports to backends.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Internet -> Router (ECMP) -> L4 node 1 -> Backend pool
                          -> L4 node 2
                          -> L4 node 3
Node 2 dies -> router rehashes some flows; consistent hashing on the LB layer
sends those flows to the same backend as before, so most connections survive.
  • Active-passive: simple, tested failover required, wastes capacity.
  • DNS multi-IP: failover bounded by TTL and client behaviour.
  • ECMP: needs network team and BGP; flows rehash when the node set changes, so the LB layer must map a flow to the same backend (consistent hashing or connection syncing).
  • Capacity: L7 LBs scale over minutes, so a 10x surge can exceed current capacity (pre-warm for planned events). Ephemeral ports: about 64k per backend IP:port, causing connect failures at high rates without keepalive.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Active-passive without ever testing failover.
  • Forgetting port and connection limits.
  • Relying on DNS TTL for failover timing.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why does consistent hashing matter in the LB layer? -> A rehash otherwise sends mid-connection packets to a different backend and resets connections.
  2. How does DNS failover compare? -> Slow (TTL, caches, clients that ignore TTL).
  3. How would you test? -> Kill an LB node under load, measure connection resets and recovery time.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer says "have two load balancers". The senior picks a pattern with failover time, describes flow stickiness under node loss and lists the limits.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A VRRP pair that was never failed over in production had a stale firewall rule on the standby; the first real failure became a 20 minute outage.

questions.contextHtml:
Behind an ALB (idle timeout 60 s), a Node.js service sees rare, unreproducible 502s: about 0.03% of requests, more at low traffic hours. Access log excerpt:

elb_status=502 target_status=- request_processing_time=0.000 target_processing_time=-1 response_processing_time=-1 error_reason=-

App CPU 20%, no exceptions logged. The Node server uses the default keep-alive timeout of 5 s. Someone proposes adding retries in the client and someone else proposes upgrading Node.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Treats it as random network noise and adds client retries, which hides the issue and risks duplicates for POSTs.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is target_status empty (backend never replied)? Does the rate rise when traffic is low (connections sitting idle)? What are keepalive settings on both sides?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Raise the backend keep-alive timeout above the LB idle timeout; low risk, immediate.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) backend closes idle connection first and the LB reuses it, (b) a backend crash, (c) security group or NAT idle drop, (d) oversized headers.
  4. How I'd verify: target_status=- with target_processing_time=-1 means no response from target. Check server.keepAliveTimeout (5 s) versus the 60 s ALB setting; packet capture on the backend shows FIN from the app just before a request arrives (race).
  5. Root cause: The ALB keeps connections to targets idle up to 60 s; the app closes at 5 s. When the LB sends a request on a connection the app just closed, the app resets it and the LB returns 502. Low traffic means more idle connections, hence more 502s.
  6. Fix:
server.keepAliveTimeout = 65000   // > ALB idle 60 s
server.headersTimeout  = 66000   // must be above keepAliveTimeout in Node

(Verify the exact values against your Node version.) Rule: backend keep-alive timeout must exceed the LB idle timeout. 7. Prevention: Template for every service; alert on LB-generated 502/504 versus target 5xx separately; load test at low QPS too. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not just add client retries; for POST they cause double actions. Higher keep-alive holds more idle sockets (cheap at this scale).

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• 504 instead of 502? -> Backend too slow, check timeouts and slow queries.
  • Does NGINX in the middle change this? -> The same rule applies at every hop: downstream idle timeout must exceed upstream.
  • Why was the red herring (Node upgrade) wrong? -> The timing correlation with low traffic points to idle connections.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A rare 502 haunted a team for two quarters. The fix was one config number. They then added the rule to the service template.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: random network, add retries.
  • Hire: connects 502 with idle timeout mismatch.
  • Strong hire: reads the log fields, gives the rule for every hop, distinguishes LB vs app errors.

questions.contextHtml:
A new gRPC service runs on 40 pods behind a Kubernetes Service and an L4 NLB. Under 20,000 calls/s:

pod        cpu   rps
pod-17     95%   9,800
pod-03     12%     300
... (38 others)  8-12%  ~250 each

The 25 client instances each open one HTTP/2 connection. Autoscaler adds pods but the hot pod stays hot. A teammate says the LB algorithm is broken and wants to switch to least connections.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Tweaks the algorithm. Least connections at L4 still balances connections; with one connection per client it cannot spread requests.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: How many client connections exist? Are clients long-lived and multiplexing? Is balancing L4 or L7? Is there a mesh or a client library with balancing?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Restart or drain the hot pod's connections (forces re-pick) and set a max connection age on the server so connections recycle.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) L4 balances connections and HTTP/2 multiplexes many requests on one connection, (b) one client sends most traffic, (c) pod-17 is a noisy node, (d) hashing skew.
  4. How I'd verify: count connections per pod (ss -tn state established '( sport = :50051 )' | wc -l), requests per connection from metrics, source IPs of the connections on pod-17.
  5. Root cause: Only about 25 connections exist across 40 pods; a few carry most of the load and the balancer made its decision once at connect time.
  6. Fix: Short term: server MAX_CONNECTION_AGE with grace (gRPC server option) so clients reconnect and spread. Long term: L7 balancing (Envoy or an L7 LB that understands gRPC) or client-side balancing (headless Service with a round_robin policy and DNS refresh); many mesh setups do this by default.
  7. Prevention: Per-pod request skew alert; load test with the real client topology, not a single load generator.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Client-side balancing needs client updates and discovery; L7 adds a hop of about 1 ms. I would not scale pods up, which does not move traffic.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Connection age too short? -> Reconnect churn and handshake cost; pick minutes with jitter.
  • Streams that last hours? -> Balance at stream creation and cap stream lifetime.
  • Why does it work with REST at L4? -> HTTP/1.1 clients open many connections, so connection balancing is request-like.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A migration from REST to gRPC moved cost to one pod per client group. Putting an L7 proxy in front evened CPU to within 10%.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: tunes the algorithm.
  • Hire: explains HTTP/2 multiplexing versus L4.
  • Strong hire: gives three fixes with trade-offs, verifies with connection counts and adds skew alerts.

questions.contextHtml: Three regions (Mumbai, Singapore, Frankfurt) each serve about 90,000 requests/s at peak. Each region is provisioned for 120,000 requests/s. Finance asks to remove "wasted capacity". The SLO requires surviving the loss of one region. Mumbai failed last quarter for 25 minutes and the surviving regions hit 100% CPU, latency tripled. Data is regional with async replication to the others.
questions.promptHtml: What utilisation do you allow, what do you do about the data, and what is reversible?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Active-active across three regions is naturally resilient." Ignores the capacity math and write handling.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is traffic equal? Is it acceptable to degrade (disable non-critical features) in a failover? What RPO is required? Who is each user's home region?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Not an incident; I validate the failover plan. Losing Mumbai sends 90,000 to the other two: 45,000 each, so each carries 135,000, over the 120,000 limit (112%).
  3. Hypotheses (options): (a) buy to 135,000 per region (66% utilisation at peak), (b) cut peak with load shedding and a degrade mode, (c) add a fourth region, lowering N-1 headroom to 33% each, (d) cache more at the edge.
  4. How I'd verify: game-day region evacuation at 10% steps; measure per-region saturation and database replication lag.
  5. Root cause: The rule: with N regions each at utilisation u, survivors need u x N/(N-1) <= 1; for N=3 u <= 66%, for N=2 u <= 50%. Current u is 75%.
  6. Fix: Plan for 135,000 capacity or shed features: degrade (search suggestions, recommendations) to bring failover demand under 120,000, about 11% less. Handle data: user data has a home region; on failover, route reads to a replica and decide whether writes fail over (risk of replication-lag data loss) or are queued.
  7. Prevention: Quarterly evacuation drills, capacity alert at 60% sustained, traffic shifting tool with 10% steps.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Running hot to save cost makes a regional failure a global outage. Multi-region writes are a one-way door (conflict resolution); I keep single-writer per user. Cost of spare capacity is the price of the SLO.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• DNS TTL 300 s so failover takes 5 minutes? -> Use anycast or a global front door with health-based routing; lower TTL helps partly.
  • Failover causes a cold cache stampede? -> Pre-warm and use request coalescing.
  • Mumbai returns; fail back? -> Gradually, with replication caught up.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A company cut spare capacity to 20% and lost one region. The two survivors fell over from retry load within five minutes, turning a regional incident into a global one.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: says "active-active handles it".
  • Hire: computes N/(N-1) headroom.
  • Strong hire: adds degrade mode, data and write routing, drills, and reversible vs one-way framing.

questions.contextHtml:
A pool of 20 JVM API nodes uses least_conn in two LB nodes. During a rolling deploy, each time a new node joins it gets a burst of connections, goes to 100% CPU for 90 s (cold JIT), p99 on that node hits 8 s, some requests time out, and the retries make neighbours busy too:

t=0   node-21 joins, active_conn=0   (others ~180)
t=3s  node-21 active_conn=410  cpu 100%
t=40s timeouts, LB retries onto node-04 .. node-09
t=90s node-21 cpu 35%

A teammate wants more nodes. Another says switch to round robin.
questions.promptHtml: Why does this happen and what do you change?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Switches algorithm without addressing warm-up, or just scales out.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Does the LB support slow start? Do clients/LB retry, and how many? Is the cold start due to JIT and cache fill? Does the readiness probe pass before the app is warm?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Enable slow start (ramp over 60 to 90 s) and reduce retries; temporarily deploy more slowly (one node at a time).
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) least connections favours the empty new node (it looks idle), (b) cold JVM can't handle the share, (c) retries amplify, (d) readiness passes too early.
  4. How I'd verify: conn count per node at join time; JIT compile and GC logs on the new node; retry rate metric at LB.
  5. Root cause: Least connections sends all new requests to the node with the lowest count, which is the unwarmed node. Two LB nodes acting on the same stale view add to the herd.
  6. Fix: Slow start (ALB slow start mode, nginx slow_start, Envoy slow start window) so weight ramps from low; warm-up endpoint that runs representative traffic before readiness; retry budget (for example at most 20% extra) with jittered backoff; P2C reduces herding.
  7. Prevention: Canary new nodes with 1% traffic; alert on per-node p99 skew; deploy health gating based on latency.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Slow start makes deploys slower and temporarily shifts load to old nodes (needs headroom). Round robin would also give the new node 1/20 right away, but ignores slow requests later. I'd not add retries.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• AOT or native image? -> Reduces cold start; trade-offs in build and peak performance.
  • Autoscaling adds nodes at the spike's peak? -> Warm-up makes scale-out slow; use predictive scaling.
  • Why do retries matter here? -> A retry of a timed-out request adds load just where capacity is short: a retry storm.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: Every deploy caused a mini incident for months. Slow start plus a warm-up call removed it, and nobody noticed the deploys anymore.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: scales out or changes algorithm only.
  • Hire: identifies empty-node attraction and cold start; proposes slow start.
  • Strong hire: also retry budgets, P2C, warm-up before readiness and canary gating.
